items.title: lyramakesmusic/neuron-explorer
items.description: Steering-first neuron explorer for Qwen3.5-4B: push every MLP neuron, keep every rollout, browse the results
items.readme:
# neuron explorer

Steering-first neuron explorer for Qwen3.5-4B. Every MLP neuron in a layer is pushed up and down on a few prompts, every
rollout is kept, and the explorer lays the results out over a 3D view of the model.

![neuron explorer](explorer.png)

## Explorer

    uv sync
    uv run python explorer/server.py        # http://localhost:8791

Reads sweep runs from `runs/` and per-layer stats from `stats/`, both produced by the sweep below; the caches in
`explorer/cache/` ship with the repo. Loads Qwen3.5-4B locally (MPS, CUDA or CPU) for live
steered chat, lens, connections and live inference over your own text.

- **map**: the model's layers in perspective, attention and MLP per layer, one point per neuron. Hover shows a neuron's
  steer lens and logit lens; click opens it; click a layer's label to view its sheet face-on. `writes` places
  neurons with similar down-projection columns next to each other.
- **list**: units ranked by word-cluster mass against random-direction controls; `lens` searches the steer and logit
  lenses for a token, `fires` runs your text through the model and filters neurons by activation.
- **neuron**: steered rollouts per prompt and dose, a three-column multi-turn steered chat (−, 0, +), lens and
  connections, and a name.
- **embeddings**: UMAP of a layer's rollouts, coloured by neuron, prompt, dose or kind.
- **Claude** (fourth neuron-panel tab, or the right-edge handle): a chat running the `claude` CLI (installed and
  logged in) with the explorer as an MCP server (`explorer/agent_mcp.py`). It reads neurons, cones and lenses, runs the
  live model (steering, activations, next-token logprobs, ablations), moves the map, list and highlights, and has file
  tools and a shell in your home folder. Its prompt is `explorer/agent_prompt.md` plus `explorer/agent_methodology.md`, and
  `explorer/agent_prompt.local.md` when present (untracked, for your own additions);
  `EXPLORER_CLAUDE_MODEL` picks the model. The server answers only pages and tools on this machine.

## Sweep

Runs on a CUDA 13 GPU pod with the steering fork of vLLM ([RhizoNymph/vllm](https://github.com/RhizoNymph/vllm)).

    bash sweep/setup_pod.sh                                   # fork, deps, model; writes /workspace/env.sh
    python sweep/neuron_stats.py --layers 22 --tokens 2000000 --out stats/q35-4b
    python sweep/steer_sweep.py --stats stats/q35-4b_L22.npz --design main_rel --dose-unit rel \
        --neurons all --random-controls 256 --run q35-4b-L22
    sweep/run_depth.sh "4 9 13 17" 384 64                     # random-subset sweep across several layers

`main_rel` doses are fractions of the median residual norm leaving the layer: {who, snake, orange} × {−0.7, +0.5, +0.8}
and {free} × {+3}, plus one unsteered baseline per prompt.

| script | output |
|---|---|
| `sweep/neuron_stats.py` | per-neuron activation extremes by sign regime, down columns, residual norms |
| `sweep/steer_sweep.py` | `runs/<run>.jsonl`: text, token ids, logprobs, top-k per step; optional activation captures |
| `sweep/rank.py` | `runs/<run>.units.jsonl`: distinctive words, cluster mass, percentile against controls |
| `sweep/steer_lens.py` | `stats/steer_lens_L{l}.npz`: next-token Δlogprob and KL for ±0.8 pushes on every neuron |
| `sweep/depth_report.py` | `runs/depth_report.json`: per-layer share of neurons above controls, coherence, top units |
| `sweep/shift.py` | word-shift score against controls, all words counted |
| `sweep/merge_runs.py` | joins sharded runs of one layer |
| `sweep/check_equivalence.py` | HF vs vLLM steering and capture agreement |
| `sweep/bench.py`, `sweep/peek.py` | throughput conditions; terminal views of a run |
| `explorer/build_embeddings.py` | `runs/<run>.umap.json` |
| `explorer/build_layout.py` | `explorer/cache/layout_writes.npz` |
| `explorer/build_connections.py` | `explorer/cache/connections.npz`: each neuron's 24 strongest direct-path links up and down |
| `sweep/capture_prefill.py` | `captures/<run>.mlp_in.npy`: MLP input at the last prompt token at the run's capture layers, steered |

`research_log.md` holds the findings and reasoning; `NOTES.md` the source notes.

items.title: morganlinton/BeautifulRust
items.description: A Claude Code plugin that teaches Claude to write idiomatic, robust Rust
items.readme: # Beautiful Rust Three standard [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) and a lints config that teach coding agents to write, review, port, and enforce idiomatic Rust: - **`rust-best-practices`** loads whenever an agent writes or changes Rust, and steers it toward idiomatic, robust, maintainable code. - **`rust-review`** reviews existing Rust code, a file, a crate, or a diff, and writes a prioritized report where every finding cites the rule it breaks and shows the fix. - **`rust-port`** ports C, C++, Python, Go, or JavaScript to idiomatic Rust with the same behavior, porting the original tests first so you can prove the two match. - **`lints/`** is a drop-in clippy configuration that enforces the machine-checkable rules in CI. They work with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and any other agent that reads the Agent Skills format. Every code example in the skills compiles on stable Rust, and every lint in the config was checked against current clippy. The guidance is distilled from five sources, with a condensed digest of each bundled in the skill so the agent can consult the original reasoning when it needs to: - [Google Rust Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/rustguide.html) - [Rust API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/) (official rust-lang checklist) - [Effective Rust](https://www.lurklurk.org/effective-rust/) by David Drysdale - [Rust Design Patterns](https://rust-unofficial.github.io/patterns/) (idioms, patterns, anti-patterns) - [Microsoft Pragmatic Rust Guidelines](https://microsoft.github.io/rust-guidelines/) Where the sources disagree, the skill picks a side and says why. ## What it changes Asked for a small semver-parsing library, an agent without the skill produced working code with public fields, no `# Errors` docs, and `unwrap()` in its doc examples. With the skill, the same agent kept the fields private, documented failure modes, and wrote doc examples users can copy safely. Condensed from those two runs: ```rust // Without the skill /// A semantic version. The fields are public for convenience. pub struct Version { pub major: u64, pub minor: u64, pub patch: u64, pub pre: Vec, pub build: Vec, } impl Version { /// Parses a version string. /// /// ``` /// let v = Version::parse("1.2.3").unwrap(); /// ``` pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result { /* ... */ } } ``` ```rust // With the skill /// A semantic version. Equality, hashing, and ordering ignore build metadata. pub struct Version { major: u64, minor: u64, patch: u64, pre: Vec, build: Vec, } impl Version { /// Parses a version string according to SemVer 2.0.0. /// /// # Errors /// /// Returns [`ParseVersionError`] if the string is empty, a numeric part has a /// leading zero or overflows `u64`, or an identifier contains invalid characters. /// /// ``` /// # use semver_lite::Version; /// # fn main() -> Result<(), semver_lite::ParseVersionError> { /// let v = Version::parse("1.2.3-beta.1")?; /// assert_eq!(v.major(), 1); /// # Ok(()) /// # } /// ``` pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result { /* ... */ } /// Returns the major version number. pub fn major(&self) -> u64 { self.major } } ``` Across three test tasks (a library, a CLI, and refactoring a messy module), the skill passed 29 of 30 checks against 24 of 30 without it. See [Testing the skills](#testing-the-skills). ## Install Each skill is a folder under `skills/`: `rust-best-practices/`, `rust-review/`, and `rust-port/`. Every option below puts those folders where your agent looks for skills. Install all three; the review and port skills lean on the best-practices skill for style. ### Any agent, one command The [`skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) installer supports most agents (Node 22.20 or later): ```bash npx skills add morganlinton/BeautifulRust ``` Add `-g` to install for your user instead of the current project, or `-a ` to pick an agent, such as `-a codex` or `-a cursor`. ### Claude Code Install it as a plugin so updates arrive with one command: ```bash claude plugin install beautiful-rust --marketplace morganlinton/BeautifulRust ``` Inside a session, the same thing is: ``` /plugin marketplace add morganlinton/BeautifulRust /plugin install beautiful-rust@beautiful-rust ``` This installs all three skills. They appear as `/beautiful-rust:rust-best-practices`, `/beautiful-rust:rust-review`, and `/beautiful-rust:rust-port`, though you rarely need to call them, since they trigger on their own. To try it for one session without installing, clone the repo and run `claude --plugin-dir ./BeautifulRust`. ### GitHub Copilot With GitHub CLI 2.90 or later: ```bash gh skill install morganlinton/BeautifulRust rust-best-practices gh skill install morganlinton/BeautifulRust rust-review gh skill install morganlinton/BeautifulRust rust-port ``` This installs into the current project by default. Add `--scope user` to install for your user, or `--agent ` to install for a different agent. ### Gemini CLI ```bash gemini skills install https://github.com/morganlinton/BeautifulRust --path skills/rust-best-practices gemini skills install https://github.com/morganlinton/BeautifulRust --path skills/rust-review gemini skills install https://github.com/morganlinton/BeautifulRust --path skills/rust-port ``` ### OpenAI Codex, Cursor, or anything else: copy the folder Clone the repo and copy the three skill folders into your agent's skills directory. Most agents now read the shared `.agents/skills/` location: ```bash git clone https://github.com/morganlinton/BeautifulRust mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills cp -R BeautifulRust/skills/rust-* ~/.agents/skills/ ``` | Agent | User directory | Project directory | |---|---|---| | Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/` | `.claude/skills/` | | OpenAI Codex | `~/.agents/skills/` | `.agents/skills/` | | GitHub Copilot | `~/.copilot/skills/` or `~/.agents/skills/` | `.github/skills/` or `.agents/skills/` | | Cursor | `~/.cursor/skills/` or `~/.agents/skills/` | `.cursor/skills/` or `.agents/skills/` | | Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/skills/` or `~/.agents/skills/` | `.gemini/skills/` or `.agents/skills/` | Claude Code does not read `.agents/skills/`, so use its own directory or the plugin. Restart the agent if the skill doesn't show up right away. ### claude.ai claude.ai takes one zip per skill, with the skill folder as the zip root: ```bash cd skills zip -r ../rust-best-practices.zip rust-best-practices -x '*.DS_Store' -x '*/evals/*' zip -r ../rust-review.zip rust-review -x '*.DS_Store' -x '*/evals/*' zip -r ../rust-port.zip rust-port -x '*.DS_Store' -x '*/evals/*' ``` Upload each under **Customize > Skills**. Code execution must be enabled first. ## Reviewing existing code Ask your agent to review a file, crate, or diff, for example "review src/parser.rs" or "what would you change in this PR". The `rust-review` skill runs `cargo fmt`, `clippy`, and the tests when a toolchain is available, then writes a report with three tiers: must fix, should fix, and consider. Every finding gives a `file:line` location, the rule it breaks with its source (an API Guidelines code such as `C-GETTER`, an Effective Rust item, a Microsoft guideline, or a clippy lint), and the smallest code change that fixes it. Each report ends with what the code already does well. [`examples/review-inventory.md`](examples/review-inventory.md) is a real review the skill produced for the deliberately messy module in the eval cases. ## Porting code to Rust Ask your agent to port a module, for example "port parser.c to Rust" or "rewrite this Python service in Rust". The `rust-port` skill reads the original and its tests, ports the tests first, designs a Rust API instead of transliterating the original, and verifies with `cargo test` and `clippy`. It maps each language's habits to their Rust equivalents: `NULL` and `None` to `Option`, error codes and exceptions to an error enum, out-parameters to return values, flag ints and magic strings to typed enums and options, and dict insertion order to an ordered collection instead of a `HashMap` that would silently reorder output. Each port comes with a `PORTING.md` that maps the old API and tests to the new ones and lists every deliberate difference. ## Enforcing the rules with clippy The skills teach the rules; the lints keep them from slipping back in. Copy [`lints/clippy.toml`](lints/clippy.toml) next to your `Cargo.toml` and paste the `[lints]` block from [`lints/lints.toml`](lints/lints.toml) into it, then run: ```bash cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings ``` It flags `unwrap()` outside tests, `unsafe` blocks without a `// SAFETY:` comment, `#[allow]` without a reason, any `bool` function parameter, silent lossy `as` casts, missing `# Errors` and `# Panics` docs, and leftover `dbg!` and `todo!`. Lints marked `[lib]` in the file are for libraries, and applications can drop them. Every lint in the table is proven to fire. [`lints/check/`](lints/check/src/lib.rs) is a small crate with one deliberate violation per lint, and this script runs clippy on it from the repo root: ```bash bash scripts/check-lints.sh ``` It fails if a lint stops firing, if something unexpected fires, or if the check crate's copy of the table drifts from `lints/lints.toml`. `allow_attributes` and `allow_attributes_without_reason` need `rust-version = "1.81"` or later, because clippy switches them off for crates that can't use `#[expect]`. ## What the writing skill covers `skills/rust-best-practices/SKILL.md` is about 500 lines, organized so an agent can scan it while coding: 1. Mindset: Rust-shaped code, invalid states unrepresentable, application vs library 2. Pre-handback checklist: fmt, clippy with `-D warnings`, test, doc; lint policy 3. Ownership and borrowing: what to do instead of cloning for the borrow checker 4. Types and API design: naming, newtypes, common traits, builders, visibility, generics vs `dyn` 5. Errors and panics: `Option` vs `Result` vs panic, library vs application error types 6. Everyday idioms: iterators, combinators, `format!`, imports, drop guards 7. Concurrency and async: `Send` assertions, lock discipline, `async fn`, yield points 8. Unsafe and FFI: when it's allowed, `SAFETY:` comments, soundness, bindgen 9. Crates, modules, dependencies: workspace layout, features, semver 10. Documentation and comments 11. Tests 12. Performance, in order 13. Final checklist `skills/rust-best-practices/references/` holds one digest per source for deeper lookups. ## Layout ``` BeautifulRust/ ├── .claude-plugin/ │ ├── plugin.json plugin manifest │ └── marketplace.json lets this repo act as its own marketplace ├── skills/ │ ├── rust-best-practices/ writing skill │ │ ├── SKILL.md │ │ ├── references/ one digest per source │ │ └── evals/ │ ├── rust-review/ review skill │ │ ├── SKILL.md │ │ └── evals/ │ └── rust-port/ porting skill │ ├── SKILL.md │ └── evals/ a C module and a Python module to port ├── lints/ │ ├── lints.toml [lints] block for Cargo.toml │ ├── clippy.toml clippy thresholds │ └── check/ one deliberate violation per lint ├── scripts/ │ ├── check-skill.py validates skills, evals, and manifests │ └── check-lints.sh proves every lint in the table fires ├── examples/ │ └── review-inventory.md a real review report ├── CHANGELOG.md ├── CONTRIBUTING.md └── README.md ``` ## Testing the skills `skills/rust-best-practices/evals/` holds three test cases in the layout `claude plugin eval` reads: a library API design task, an application CLI task, and a refactor-this-module task with an input file. Each case has the prompt, a description of a good result, and one assertion per file under `graders/`. Run them with and without the skill from the skill directory: ```bash claude plugin eval . --allow-tools Write,Edit,Bash --scaffold ``` `skills/rust-review/evals/` holds a review case for the same messy module, and `skills/rust-port/evals/` holds a C module and a Python module to port, each with its original test suite. Run them the same way from each skill's directory. These are real model runs and are billed. In the last comparison the writing skill passed 29 of 30 assertions against 24 of 30 without it, at roughly a third more tokens per task. The review skill passed 11 of 12 against 7 of 12, and the porting skill 22 of 22 against 19 of 22. ## Updating Edit the skill, bump `version` in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, commit, and push. Claude Code plugin users pick up the new version with: ```bash claude plugin update beautiful-rust ``` Anyone who copied the folder or used an installer re-runs the install command. Record each release in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md). Validate before pushing. `python3 scripts/check-skill.py` checks skill frontmatter, links, eval cases, and plugin manifests. Pass `--json` for machine-readable output. ```bash python3 scripts/check-skill.py claude plugin validate . ``` ## Contributing Issues and pull requests are welcome. Every rule needs a published source; see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to propose a rule, report a review false positive, or add an eval case. ## Sources and attribution The guidance in this skill is a synthesis. The five digests in `skills/rust-best-practices/references/` are paraphrased summaries written for this project; they restate each source's advice in condensed form and link back to the original. Read the originals for the full reasoning. | Source | Author | License | |---|---|---| | [Google Rust Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/rustguide.html) | Google | CC BY 3.0 | | [Rust API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/) | The Rust Project | MIT or Apache-2.0 | | [Effective Rust](https://www.lurklurk.org/effective-rust/) | David Drysdale, published by O'Reilly | CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (online edition) | | [Rust Design Patterns](https://rust-unofficial.github.io/patterns/) | rust-unofficial contributors | MPL-2.0 | | [Pragmatic Rust Guidelines](https://microsoft.github.io/rust-guidelines/) | Microsoft | MIT | The skill text, the digests, the banner, and the generator script in this repository are MIT licensed (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). The crab is a crab, not the Rust mascot. ## License MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

items.title: NVIDIA/flare-local-inference
items.readme: > **Coding agents:** skip this README and read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) directly. Flare is a local inference server for NVIDIA SM120/SM121 GPUs, built for long conversations, coding agents, and repeated tool use. Its goal is to make the memory, bandwidth, and compute in workstations and compact systems such as DGX Spark go further, while keeping generation responsive. This is a research prototype, and is made available via open-source to enable technical collaboration and collect early feedback. The design rests on a few principles: - **Embrace the standard PyTorch ecosystem at build time; serve from Rust.** Ignition uses PyTorch, Transformers, and FlashInfer/b12x to load models, tune kernels, compile forwards, and capture CUDA graphs into a runtime package. Helios, the Rust runtime, serves that package without Python. Compilation and graph capture finish before serving. - **Build on the model ecosystem.** Reuse canonical model implementations wherever their dataflow fits, and specialize the parts that need different layouts or execution. Model development keeps the tools and libraries that make the Python ecosystem productive. - **Make memory and state explicit.** Plan buffers and execution capacities ahead of time. Treat conversation state—including recurrent state alongside KV caches—as a whole, so reuse, branching, and resuming preserve it correctly. - **Keep the runtime small and shared.** Model recipes own model computation; the runtime owns scheduling, cache storage, and request handling. A focused hardware and kernel stack keeps those boundaries manageable. [vLLM](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/) covers a much broader range of models, hardware, and deployment patterns. Flare trades that breadth for a focused serving contract around selected models and local workloads. Flare is not, and will never, be a replacement for production inference englines like vLLM. Think of Flare as a specialized option when its hardware and model coverage fit your machine. Start with [model preparation and serving](docs/model-preparation.md). See the [CLI guide](docs/cli-design.md) for configuration and the [core design](docs/core-design.md) for the architectural reasoning.

items.readme:
A community-built phone app for Clean Your TV.
Anyone can clean up their TV: no laptop, no coding agent, no cables.

Download · Get it with Obtainium · How it works · Is it safe? · Supported TVs
Obtainium follows this app's GitHub releases and updates it by itself.

## How it works | 1. Connect | 2. Analyse | 3. Clean | | :-: | :-: | :-: | | | | | | The app finds your TV on the Wi-Fi and shows you how to let the phone in with the remote. | It reads what is on the TV and shows the plan: what goes off and what stays. Nothing changes yet. | Tap "Make it clean". A restore point first, then the clutter goes and the new home screen comes on. | **You need** an Android phone (Android 9 or newer, with a screen lock) on the same Wi-Fi as the TV. [Download the APK](https://github.com/udhaykumarbala/cleanyourtv-app/releases/latest) and open it to install. Connecting takes about a minute (you switch on network debugging with the remote; the app shows you how), and the whole clean-up about five minutes. Come back any time to put an app back, check for leftovers after a TV update, change the dock or the look, or undo everything. ## Two ways to clean your TV [Clean Your TV](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv) gives any Android TV a calm, ad-free home screen and switches off the bloat, using lists tested by its community. On its own it needs a computer: you run its scripts, or hand its prompt to a coding agent. This app does the whole job from your phone. | | Clean Your TV repo | **Clean Your TV app** (this repo) | | :- | :- | :- | | **You need** | A computer with ADB, or a coding agent such as Claude Code | **Just an Android phone** on the same Wi-Fi as the TV | | **You do** | Run the scripts, or give the prompt to the agent | **Tap Start, check the plan, tap "Make it clean"** | | **Made for** | Tinkerers, themes and new TV lists | **Everyone**: you, your parents, your friends | Both give you the same Clean Your TV home screen and the same community TV lists, switch apps off without uninstalling them, and keep a way back for every change. ## Safe by design - **You see every step.** Nothing runs until you have seen the plan, and Customise shows every command the app would send, in order. - **Nothing is deleted.** Apps are switched off for the main user, so each one can come back. Wi-Fi, the Play Store, the remote, the TV's inputs and the parts Android needs are protected and never touched; accessibility, casting, voice and updates go off only if you choose. - **Undo anything.** Put back one app or everything from the restore point. "Save a copy" exports plain restore scripts that work from any computer with adb, even without this app. - **A watchdog on the TV.** If the phone does not confirm the new home screen within 150 seconds (the Wi-Fi drops, the phone dies), the TV puts its own home screen back by itself. - **Careful where it counts.** On TVs where switching the home screen is known to cause trouble, the app does the clean-up only and tells you why. - **Private.** No accounts, no analytics, no ads. The app talks to your TV and, only when you ask, to GitHub for updates. Network debugging is switched off again at the end unless you keep it on. ## Supported TVs **131 TV models from 46 brands**, from the Clean Your TV community lists: TCL, Sony, Xiaomi, Hisense, Philips, Amazon Fire TV, Panasonic, XGIMI, BenQ, NVIDIA Shield, onn, Google and many more, on Android TV, Google TV and Fire OS. A model nobody has listed yet still gets a careful clean-up based on its brand.
The details - **Profiles:** TCL (24 models), Sony (17), Xiaomi (17), Hisense, Philips, Amazon Fire TV, Panasonic, XGIMI, BenQ, NVIDIA Shield, Skyworth, Haier, CHiQ, onn, Google, Vestel-made sets (JVC, Toshiba, Cecotec), the Freebox Player and more, on Android TV, Google TV, Fire OS and TCL's China builds. Each profile names who tested it. - **Brand fallback:** for Amazon, Hisense, Panasonic, Philips, Sony, TCL, XGIMI and Xiaomi models without a profile, the app switches off only what every profile of that brand agrees on, and says it is being careful. More can be switched off by hand under Customise. - **Other Android TVs** get the home screen, and the app suggests only what it is sure about. - **Clean-up only** (the TV keeps its own home screen, and the app says why): Fire TV, TCL's China builds, Android 7, vendor home screens the app does not know, Chromecast with Google TV and the Google TV Streamer (the switch would cost casting), the Kalley and PRISM+ sets whose setup wizard returns at every boot, and TVs whose setup wizard has to stay on. - **Network debugging:** the TV needs ADB over the network (port 5555). On TVs that only offer Wireless debugging with a pairing code, pair once from a computer; the app shows the three commands.
**Your TV is not listed?** TV lists live in Clean Your TV, so they help everyone, with or without the app. Add yours there by following its [contributing guide](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md), and the app picks it up in its next release. See also [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#propose-a-tv-profile). ## Built on Clean Your TV - The home screen is the [Clean Your TV launcher](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/tree/main/launcher) by [Gathin](https://github.com/Gathin23). The app carries it inside, built from its source. - New TV lists and launcher versions from Clean Your TV reach the app in its updates. The app is a community project; news about Clean Your TV itself comes from [@gathint](https://x.com/gathint). - The Clean Your TV name and the app's package IDs under `tv.cleanyour` (from `cleanyour.tv`) are used with Gathin's permission. - Something wrong in the app itself? [Open an issue here](https://github.com/udhaykumarbala/cleanyourtv-app/issues). Security issues: see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
Privacy in detail - No accounts, no analytics, no advertising, no crash reporting service. - On your home network the app talks only to the TV you pick (ADB on port 5555) and listens for TVs announcing themselves (mDNS). - On the internet it talks only to GitHub, and only when you ask: "Check for updates" makes one request for the latest release, and an optional add-on downloads from its GitHub release. The launcher and the TV progress screen are inside the APK, so a normal setup makes no internet request at all. - The key the TV trusts lives in the phone's Android Keystore and never leaves the phone. Restore points stay on the phone unless you save a copy yourself. - "Report a problem" and "Help add this TV" show the whole report first, remove addresses, serial numbers, keys and codes, and send nothing themselves: you share it or post it on GitHub. - Permissions: internet, network state, Wi-Fi multicast (to find the TV), a foreground service while it works on the TV, notifications and the screen lock prompt. No location, storage, camera or contacts. - The full policy: [PRIVACY.md](PRIVACY.md), published at [cleanyour.tv/app/android/privacy](https://cleanyour.tv/app/android/privacy).
Check the download Every release is signed by the same key, whose certificate SHA-256 is (also in [docs/release-signer.sha256](docs/release-signer.sha256)): ``` eaf7af3867bb29ff4bb038854842c93f42ffe4198a087e611cb18f925201cd65 ``` ```bash sha256sum cleanyourtv-0.2.0.apk # compare with the release notes apksigner verify --print-certs cleanyourtv-0.2.0.apk ``` Android refuses an update signed by any other key, so after the first install every update is checked for you. The build is reproducible: for every release tag CI builds the unsigned APK from the public source, and `scripts/verify-release.sh` checks that the published APK is exactly that build plus a signature.
## For developers ```bash git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/udhaykumarbala/cleanyourtv-app.git cd cleanyourtv-app ./gradlew check assembleDebug # JDK 21 and the Android SDK ``` A Kotlin and Jetpack Compose app that speaks ADB to the TV itself, with no computer in between. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers tests, screenshot goldens, the module rules and how releases are built and signed. How the app was designed and reviewed is in [docs/history](docs/history/README.md), and what changed in each version in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md). The app is developed with AI coding agents under human review: the maintainer set the design and reviewed and tested the app, and every change went through automated tests and review. ## Credits - [Clean Your TV](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv) by [Gathin](https://github.com/Gathin23) and its community contributors, whose launcher, clean-up lists and test reports this app is built on. - The ADB protocol code started from [dadb](https://github.com/mobile-dev-inc/dadb) by mobile.dev (Apache 2.0, see [adb/wire/NOTICE](adb/wire/NOTICE)). - The [Outfit](https://github.com/Outfitio/Outfit-Fonts) typeface (SIL Open Font License 1.1). Full list: [THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES](THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES). Licence: [MIT](LICENSE), like Clean Your TV.
